prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The current-voltage (I-V) characteristics of various MgB2 films have been studied at different magnetic fields parallel to c-axis. At fields \mu0H between 0 and 5T, vortex liquid-glass transitions were found in the I-V isotherms. Consistently, the I-V curves measured at different temperatures show a scaling behavior in the framework of quasi-two-dimension (quasi-2D) vortex glass theory. However, at \mu0 H >= 5T, a finite dissipation was observed down to the lowest temperature here, T=1.7K, and the I-V isotherms did not scale in terms of any known scaling law, of any dimensionality. We suggest that this may be caused by a mixture of \sigma band vortices and \pi band quasiparticles. Interestingly, the I-V curves at zero magnetic field can still be scaled according to the quasi-2D vortex glass formalism, indicating an equivalent effect of self-field due to persistent current and applied magnetic field.

outputs.L1: The current–voltage (I–V) characteristics of various MgB₂ films were investigated under magnetic fields applied parallel to the c-axis. For fields μ₀H between 0 and 5 T, vortex liquid–glass transitions were identified in the I–V isotherms. Consistent with this observation, the I–V curves measured at different temperatures exhibit scaling behavior within the framework of quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) vortex-glass theory. However, at μ₀H ≥ 5 T, finite dissipation persisted down to the lowest temperature investigated, T = 1.7 K, and the I–V isotherms could not be described by any known scaling law, irrespective of dimensionality. We suggest that this behavior may arise from a mixture of σ-band vortices and π-band quasiparticles. Interestingly, even at zero applied magnetic field, the I–V curves can be scaled according to the quasi-2D vortex-glass formalism, indicating that the self-field generated by the persistent current has an effect equivalent to that of an applied magnetic field.
outputs.L2: The current–voltage (I–V) behavior of several MgB₂ films was examined under magnetic fields oriented parallel to the c-axis. For fields in the range \(0 \leq \mu_0H < 5\,\text{T}\), the I–V isotherms revealed vortex liquid-to-glass transitions. Measurements taken at different temperatures also collapsed consistently within the quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) vortex-glass scaling framework. In contrast, when \(\mu_0H \geq 5\,\text{T}\), nonzero dissipation persisted down to the minimum measured temperature of \(1.7\,\text{K}\), and the isotherms could not be described by any established scaling relation, regardless of dimensionality. We propose that this behavior may arise from the coexistence of \(\sigma\)-band vortices and \(\pi\)-band quasiparticles. Notably, even in the absence of an externally applied field, the I–V data still followed quasi-2D vortex-glass scaling, suggesting that the self-field generated by persistent currents has an effect equivalent to that of an applied magnetic field.
outputs.L3:
The current–voltage (I–V) characteristics of various MgB₂ thin films were investigated under magnetic fields applied parallel to the crystallographic c-axis. For fields ranging from 0 to 5 T, the I–V isotherms exhibited clear evidence of vortex liquid-to-glass transitions. Within this field range, the temperature-dependent curves were consistent with quasi-two-dimensional vortex-glass scaling, indicating that vortex dynamics were governed predominantly by reduced-dimensional behavior.

A distinctly different response emerged at magnetic fields of 5 T and above. Under these conditions, finite dissipation persisted down to the lowest measured temperature of 1.7 K, and the I–V characteristics could not be described by any established scaling law. This high-field behavior may arise from the multiband nature of MgB₂, specifically from the coexistence of vortices associated with the σ band and quasiparticle excitations in the π band. In addition, the apparent scaling observed even in zero applied field suggests that self-fields generated by persistent currents may effectively mimic an externally applied magnetic field and thereby influence vortex dynamics.
outputs.L4:
Current–voltage characteristics of MgB₂ thin films were measured under magnetic fields applied parallel to the crystallographic c axis to investigate the transition between vortex-liquid and vortex-glass states. The data were analyzed within a quasi-two-dimensional vortex-glass scaling framework, which predicts that the current–voltage curves obtained near the glass-transition temperature can be collapsed onto universal branches corresponding to the liquid and glass regimes.

A consistent scaling collapse was obtained for magnetic fields ranging from nominally zero field up to approximately 5 T. The apparent vortex-glass behavior at zero applied field can be attributed to the film’s self-field: the transport current generates vortices even in the absence of an external magnetic field, allowing vortex dynamics to influence the current–voltage response. These results indicate that, within this field range, dissipation is governed primarily by collective vortex motion and freezing.

At fields above about 5 T, however, the quasi-2D vortex-glass scaling becomes progressively less successful. The current–voltage curves retain finite dissipation at low temperatures instead of approaching the nearly dissipationless response expected for a well-developed vortex-glass state. This behavior is likely related to the multiband superconductivity of MgB₂. In the high-field regime, the measured transport response may contain simultaneous contributions from vortices associated mainly with the strongly superconducting σ band and from quasiparticles in the more weakly superconducting π band. The resulting mixture of vortex dynamics and quasiparticle conduction is not captured by a single-band vortex-glass model, providing a natural explanation for both the residual low-temperature resistance and the breakdown of scaling above 5 T.
outputs.L5: The team consistently delivered high-quality results and met every deadline. However, continued success will depend on its ability to adapt to new challenges and remain focused on long-term goals.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the experimental findings on vortex liquid-glass transitions and I-V scaling in MgB2 films under magnetic fields parallel to the c-axis.
counterfactuals.output:
For MgB₂ films with the magnetic field applied parallel to the crystallographic \(c\)-axis, the transport measurements showed behavior consistent with a three-dimensional vortex liquid–glass transition:

- At high temperatures, the \(I\)-\(V\) curves had an ohmic low-current region, characteristic of a mobile vortex liquid.
- On cooling, the curves developed positive curvature on log–log plots and the linear resistance disappeared, indicating a pinned vortex-glass state.
- At a field-dependent glass temperature \(T_g(H)\), the \(I\)-\(V\) relation became a power law,
  \[
  E\propto J^{(z+1)/2},
  \]
  as expected for a 3D vortex-glass critical point.
- Curves above and below \(T_g\) collapsed onto two distinct branches using the Fisher–Fisher–Huse scaling form,
  \[
  \frac{E}{J}|T-T_g|^{-\nu(z-1)}
  \quad\text{vs.}\quad
  J|T-T_g|^{-2\nu}.
  \]
  This collapse was obtained over several \(c\)-axis fields.
- The fitted critical exponents were generally \(\nu\sim1\) and \(z\sim4\!-\!5\), with only modest field dependence, values typical of a 3D vortex-glass universality class.
- Increasing field lowered \(T_g\) and widened the vortex-liquid region between the glass/irreversibility line and the upper critical-field line.

Overall, the experiments supported a continuous vortex liquid-to-glass transition in \(c\)-axis fields and showed that, despite MgB₂’s two-band superconductivity, its near-transition \(I\)-\(V\) behavior can be described reasonably well by conventional 3D vortex-glass scaling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract describing current-voltage measurements of MgB2 films from zero field to above 5 T, including quasi-2D vortex-glass scaling, low-temperature dissipation, and the possible roles of σ-band vortices and π-band quasiparticles.
counterfactuals.output: Current–voltage characteristics of MgB₂ thin films were measured from zero magnetic field to fields above 5 T over a broad temperature range. In finite fields, the nonlinear response is consistent with quasi-two-dimensional vortex-glass scaling near the resistive transition, indicating a crossover from thermally activated vortex motion to a glassy regime. At low temperatures, however, a finite dissipative response persists and departs from conventional vortex-glass behavior. This residual dissipation may reflect the multiband nature of MgB₂: vortices associated primarily with the strongly superconducting σ band coexist with quasiparticles generated by suppression of the weaker π-band gap. Their combined dynamics provide a possible explanation for the high-field, low-temperature transport behavior.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: What do the I-V isotherms of MgB2 thin films reveal about vortex-glass behavior at low and high magnetic fields?
counterfactuals.output:
The MgB₂ thin-film \(I\!-\!V\) isotherms show two regimes:

- **Low magnetic fields:** The curves exhibit the characteristic vortex-glass transition—opposite curvatures on a log–log plot above and below a well-defined \(T_g\), with an approximately power-law isotherm at \(T_g\). The data can be collapsed using vortex-glass scaling, indicating a pinned, essentially three-dimensional vortex-glass phase.
- **High magnetic fields:** The curvature change and scaling collapse deteriorate or disappear. A finite low-current resistance persists, indicating thermally activated/flux-flow vortex motion rather than a true zero-resistance glass. Thus strong fields suppress the vortex-glass phase and drive the film toward a vortex-liquid or glass-crossover regime.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain why MgB2 films exhibit quasi-two-dimensional vortex-glass scaling for μ0H < 5 T but fail to follow known scaling laws at μ0H ≥ 5 T. Also discuss the significance of zero-field scaling.
counterfactuals.output:
For \( \mu_0H<5\ \text{T} \), the current–voltage curves can be collapsed with the Fisher–Fisher–Huse vortex-glass form using an effective dimensionality close to \(d=2\). This implies that the relevant vortex correlations are mainly confined to the film plane. The finite film thickness, layered electronic structure, strong anisotropic pinning, and limited transverse correlation length prevent the vortices from developing fully three-dimensional correlations, so the film behaves as a quasi-2D vortex glass.

At fields near and above \(5\ \text{T}\), a single vortex-glass scaling description no longer works. MgB\(_2\) is a two-gap superconductor: the more three-dimensional \(\pi\)-band condensate is strongly weakened by fields of a few tesla, while superconductivity increasingly resides in the anisotropic \(\sigma\) band. This produces field-dependent anisotropy, coherence lengths, pinning, and vortex viscosity, and may cause dimensional or dynamical crossovers. Consequently, there is no longer one diverging correlation length and one relaxation time—the assumptions underlying standard 2D or 3D vortex-glass scaling. Strong flux-flow contributions and broad crossover behavior can further obscure any true glass transition. Thus the high-field failure does not simply mean “no vortices”; it indicates that the dynamics cannot be represented by the conventional one-parameter glass models.

Zero-field scaling is noteworthy because an ideal zero-field sample contains no net field-induced vortex lattice. A successful collapse there points to vortex–antivortex excitations, together with residual or current-generated vortices and disorder, as the origin of the nonlinear response. It supports the importance of two-dimensional phase fluctuations and is related to a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless-like or zero-field glassy transition. It also shows that the low-field scaling is not solely a consequence of an applied-field vortex lattice. However, zero-field scaling alone is not definitive proof of a thermodynamic vortex-glass phase, since finite-size effects, self-fields, and inhomogeneity can produce similar apparent scaling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper conclusion for a study of MgB2 film I-V characteristics measured down to 1.7 K with the field aligned along the c-axis, emphasizing the crossover near 5 T and the equivalence between self-field and applied-field effects.
counterfactuals.output:
## Conclusion

We investigated the current–voltage characteristics of MgB\(_2\) thin films down to 1.7 K with the magnetic field applied parallel to the crystallographic \(c\)-axis. The measurements reveal two distinct transport regimes separated by a crossover near 5 T. Below this field, the nonlinear response is strongly influenced by the magnetic self-field generated by the transport current, whereas above approximately 5 T the externally applied field dominates and the \(I\)–\(V\) characteristics evolve more uniformly with field.

A central result is that current-induced self-field effects and applied-field effects produce equivalent changes in the transport response when compared on the basis of the total local magnetic field. This correspondence indicates that the observed nonlinearity does not require separate mechanisms for zero-field and finite-field measurements; instead, both can be understood within a common picture governed by field-dependent vortex entry, motion, and dissipation. The crossover near 5 T therefore marks a change in the relative importance of self-field and applied-field contributions rather than an abrupt change in the fundamental origin of the resistive state.

These findings show that self-field corrections are essential for interpreting low-temperature, high-current measurements of MgB\(_2\) films, particularly in the nominally low-field regime. More broadly, the equivalence between self-generated and externally imposed magnetic fields provides a consistent framework for comparing transport data across current and field scales and for assessing the vortex-dynamics limits of MgB\(_2\)-based superconducting devices.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
